body.why: It works mainly through guided imagery and the therapist's words, beginning with a short body-scan relaxation and inviting the client to feel the imagined care in the body.

exertion.why: The protocol is a short guided body-scan relaxation followed by guided imagery.

arousal.why: It begins with a body-scan relaxation and imagines parents who protect and soothe, aiming at a lasting feeling of security, although painful childhood memories may surface.

social.why: It is usually part of ongoing individual therapy, with the therapist guiding the client's imagery.

structure.why: It is a named protocol built around five qualities of ideal parents and repeated across sessions, though the developers advise tailoring the imagery to each client's attachment needs.

stance.why: It deliberately and repeatedly builds experiences of being cared for, aiming to form new inner models of oneself and others.

depth.why: It works on the early roots of insecure attachment, with the client imagining being a child with a new set of ideal parents.

perception.why: The client vividly imagines being a child with ideal parents, while keeping that imagination separate from memories of their own childhood.

guide.why: It is done with a therapist's guidance, sometimes with a recording for home practice, and is best done with a therapist trained in both the method and trauma care.

body.why: It works by turning attention inward to find feelings, thoughts or urges as parts and getting to know them.

exertion.why: The work is done by turning attention inward during therapy sessions.

arousal.why: The client steps back until they feel calm or curious toward a part, but turning toward deeply hurt parts can bring up intense trauma memories.

social.why: It is mostly individual therapy, with couple and group formats and online group programs too.

structure.why: It follows a sequence, from finding and unblending from a part to befriending protectors and, only with their permission, unburdening exiles.

stance.why: It meets parts with curiosity and compassion instead of trying to get rid of them, while helping wounded parts release the painful feelings and beliefs they carry.

depth.why: It works with exiled parts that carry old pain and shame, which means witnessing their story and bringing them out of the past.

perception.why: Attention is turned inward to parts that the client gets to know, and the therapist may speak with a part directly.

guide.why: It is normally done with a trained IFS therapist, and people with severe trauma are advised to see a licensed IFS clinician rather than rely on books or apps.

body.why: It works mainly through catching and questioning thoughts and trying new behaviors, using conversation and worksheets.

exertion.why: It is a talking therapy, with practice between sessions such as small real-life experiments and planned rewarding activities.

arousal.why: Exposure work means deliberately facing situations that make you anxious, in manageable steps, alongside planning rewarding activities.

social.why: You and a therapist agree on problems and goals together, and it is also delivered in groups, by phone and as self-help.

structure.why: Sessions follow a shared agenda with agreed goals, worksheets and between-session homework, often within a protocol for a specific problem.

stance.why: Its aim is to change unhelpful thinking and the habits that keep distress going, by checking thoughts against the evidence and trying new behaviors.

depth.why: It focuses on current problems rather than the past, working with automatic thoughts and the deeper beliefs about yourself, others and the world they are often linked to.

perception.why: Much of the work is with thoughts, which are weighed against the evidence and tested in small real-life experiments.

guide.why: You work with a therapist on agreed goals, and it is also delivered as guided or unguided self-help, including online programs.

body.why: Sessions mix conversation, metaphors and experiential exercises with short mindfulness practices, such as making room for difficult feelings.

exertion.why: Sessions mix conversation with exercises and short mindfulness practices, followed by concrete steps you commit to.

arousal.why: It combines short mindfulness practices with turning toward painful feelings, which can be uncomfortable at first.

social.why: It is delivered one to one or in groups, and also as guided or unguided self-help.

structure.why: It is organized around six linked processes, but there is no standard course, and sessions mix conversation, exercises and metaphors.

stance.why: It asks people to stop struggling with thoughts and feelings and make room for them, while committing to concrete steps toward what they value.

depth.why: Its work is with thoughts, feelings and values, through processes such as contact with the present moment and committed action.

perception.why: It mixes metaphors and values clarification with present-moment awareness exercises.

guide.why: It is delivered one to one, in groups or as self-help, which shows small benefits, while serious problems call for a qualified clinician rather than self-help alone.

body.why: It uses experiential methods to help the client feel and put into words the emotional truth behind a symptom.

exertion.why: It takes place in individual, couple or family therapy sessions focused on a specific symptom.

arousal.why: Uncovering hidden emotional learnings can be intense, and the work asks the client to feel them fully and vividly experience a contradiction.

social.why: It is used with individuals, couples and families.

structure.why: It moves through a defined sequence, from finding the emotional truth behind a symptom to juxtaposition and checking that old triggers no longer evoke the reaction.

stance.why: It aims to dissolve the old emotional learning rather than manage the symptom, though it never opposes the symptom and starts by feeling the truth behind it.

depth.why: It uncovers mostly unconscious emotional learnings, formed in response to earlier experiences, that still make a symptom feel necessary.

perception.why: It works with unrecognized emotional truths and contradicting knowledge, which the client feels, puts into words and holds in awareness at the same time.

guide.why: The therapist helps the client through each step, and a registered trial was stopped because the therapy could not be delivered in a reliable and valid way.

body.why: It is a body-based practice of stretching and tiring exercises followed by tremors that start on their own, and it does not require talking about what happened.

exertion.why: The seven exercises deliberately tire the legs and hips, including a wall sit held for a few minutes, before a phase of lying down while tremors run.

arousal.why: Its founder proposes that mild tremors help calm an over-activated nervous system, though strong emotions or memories can surface.

social.why: It is learned from a provider in private sessions or groups and then practiced alone at home.

structure.why: Each session follows a sequence of seven exercises, after which you lie down and let the tremors run for as long as feels comfortable.

stance.why: The exercises deliberately trigger tremors, and the person then lets them run, staying in charge by making them gentler or stopping.

depth.why: It is aimed at stress, tension and trauma but does not require talking about what happened, though strong emotions or memories can surface.

perception.why: The practice is physical stretching, tiring and tremoring, adjusted by shifting your legs to make the tremors gentler.

guide.why: Providers recommend learning it from a certified provider first, after which it is practiced alone as self-help.

body.why: It works through the felt sense, a vague bodily sense of a situation that is not yet in words, and lets words or images come from it.

exertion.why: It is a quiet, inward practice, often done with eyes closed.

arousal.why: It asks for gentle, open, non-judging attention, starting by clearing a space, though strong feelings can come up.

social.why: It is often done with a listener who reflects back what you say, a partner or a therapist, though it can also be done alone.

structure.why: Gendlin's six steps give a clear sequence, from clearing a space to receiving whatever comes, but with practice they become a loose guide rather than a fixed recipe.

stance.why: It gives gentle, non-judging attention to the felt sense, asks it open questions and receives whatever comes kindly.

depth.why: It works with the felt sense of a situation or problem, though turning attention inward can bring up painful memories.

perception.why: The felt sense is sensed directly in the body, but the work also means finding a word or image that fits it.

guide.why: It is usually learned from a book or a Focusing trainer and then done alone, with a trained lay listener or within therapy.

body.why: In conversation, the coach asks what is felt in the body, and the work moves through parts work, felt-sense work in the body and presence work.

exertion.why: Sessions are one-to-one conversations in which the coach slows things down.

arousal.why: The coach slows things down, the client may settle into calm, open states, and one practitioner describes it as feeling like meditating together.

social.why: It happens in one-to-one conversations in which the coach mirrors back not only the client's words but how they are said.

structure.why: Sessions start from whatever the client feels stuck on, and one conversation can move through parts work, felt-sense work, presence work and nondual awareness, which the method means to deepen step by step.

stance.why: It aims at unfoldment rather than self-improvement, helping what is already felt come fully into awareness instead of trying to fix the person.

depth.why: It works with protective parts and old emotional learnings, which its founder ties to memory reconsolidation, although as coaching it refers trauma work to therapists.

perception.why: It blends parts work with felt-sense work in the body, presence work and nondual awareness.

guide.why: It is delivered one to one by a trained Aletheia coach, a role the school describes as a nearly four-year training path.

body.why: There is no chosen object: thoughts, sounds, body feelings and daydreams are all allowed to come and go.

exertion.why: You sit comfortably, eyes open or closed.

arousal.why: It sits at the effortless, receptive end of meditation and, in research terms, is closest to training acceptance, though beginners may doze or slide into worry.

social.why: It is sitting practice, guided or alone, and Young's teaching also includes residential retreats.

structure.why: It has no object and a single instruction: let whatever happens happen, and drop any intention to control attention.

stance.why: Its one instruction is to let whatever happens happen, and mind wandering is allowed rather than corrected.

depth.why: It lets whatever happens happen, though, like any meditation, open sitting can bring up difficult emotions or memories.

perception.why: Daydreams and thoughts are allowed to come and go just as sounds and body feelings are.

guide.why: It has a single instruction and can be practiced guided or alone, as one technique among many in Young's system.

body.why: It works mainly through silently repeated phrases and the warm feeling they evoke, and in many modern jhana methods attention then rests on that pleasant feeling.

exertion.why: It is practiced sitting quietly.

arousal.why: Metta fills the mind with a warm, friendly feeling and jhana moves toward deep calm, though the first jhanas bring joy and intensive practice can bring strong energy.

social.why: You sit quietly and bring people to mind to wish them well, whether practicing on your own, in a course or on retreat.

structure.why: It uses set phrases and a fixed widening circle from self to all beings, and jhana practice follows a mapped progression of states.

stance.why: It is the deliberate cultivation of goodwill, which can be taken into absorption, rather than investigating change in experience as vipassana does.

depth.why: It cultivates goodwill toward yourself and others, though wishing yourself well can stir up grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, especially after trauma.

perception.why: You bring people to mind and silently repeat phrases, and in jhana attention is steadied, often on the breath, before resting on a pleasant feeling, an inner sign or image, or the breath and body feelings, depending on the lineage.

guide.why: Loving-kindness has been studied as self-guided practice and in courses, while deeper jhanas are usually learned on retreat with guidance from a teacher.

body.why: It observes body sensations, feelings and thoughts, sweeping attention through the body in the Goenka style or labeling each experience in the Mahasi style.

exertion.why: You sit still and observe whatever is most obvious: body sensations, sounds, emotions and thoughts.

arousal.why: Noticing experience without reacting may reduce emotional reactivity and stress, although intensive practice can bring up fear, anxiety or panic.

social.why: Daily sitting is done at home, and retreats are silent and residential.

structure.why: It uses specific techniques, such as Mahasi noting or the Goenka body sweep, and retreats follow a set plan, such as three days of breath awareness before body sweeping.

stance.why: It trains noticing what is happening and accepting it without reacting, to see clearly how experience keeps changing.

depth.why: It watches each experience arise and pass, moment by moment.

perception.why: Practitioners watch body sensations, sounds, emotions and thoughts closely, moment by moment, as they arise and pass.

guide.why: It combines daily sitting at home with residential retreats, such as Goenka's 10-day courses.

body.why: It is hard physical exercise, such as cycling, running, rowing or body-weight moves.

exertion.why: Sessions are built around repeated hard bouts that take you close to your limit, breathing hard and barely able to talk, or flat out in sprint versions.

arousal.why: During the hard bouts breathing is heavy and talking is difficult, and the aim is to challenge the heart and lungs.

social.why: Many people follow a class, a coach or an interval timer app.

structure.why: Sessions alternate set work and rest intervals, such as 4 x 4 minutes or 10 x 1 minute, between a warm-up and a cool-down.

stance.why: It deliberately pushes effort close to your limit to raise heart and lung fitness, and it is thought to help mood as well.

depth.why: It is about the effort of each session, with a gradual build-up in the number and length of hard bouts.

perception.why: You judge your effort by heart rate or by how hard it feels, on a bike, a track, a rowing machine or with body-weight moves.

guide.why: People with heart disease or other serious conditions should get medical advice first and may do best in a supervised program, and beginners are advised to build a base first.

body.why: It is a fast running game of passing and catching a disc, and players also talk through fouls and disputed calls.

exertion.why: Ultimate is a fast running game, with sprinting, cutting and jumping.

arousal.why: You play with and against other people in a fast running game, for fun and friendly competition.

social.why: Two teams play together, settle their own calls by talking them through, and often finish in a shared spirit circle.

structure.why: Sessions follow a regular schedule of warm-up, skill drills and a game, with clear team roles and a shared code for calls.

stance.why: It is played for enjoyment and health, with likely benefits from fitness, fun, friendships and a sense of competence.

depth.why: The practice is the game itself and the time spent together before and after play.

perception.why: Players pass and catch a flying disc, seven a side outdoors, and score by catching it in the end zone.

guide.why: You join a club, league or pickup game, and Ultimate is self-officiated, so players make their own calls without a referee.

body.why: It is continuous movement at a steady effort with an even rhythm, such as running, cycling, swimming or rowing.

exertion.why: You hold a steady pace for about 20 to 60 minutes while still able to speak in short sentences, at a moderate or vigorous effort.

arousal.why: It is sustained aerobic effort, and in one trial 45 minutes of running raised euphoria while also easing anxiety.

social.why: People run alone, with a friend or in a club.

structure.why: Its defining feature is an even rhythm kept up over time, with gradual increases in time or distance rather than the bursts and rests of HIIT.

stance.why: Regular training builds heart and lung fitness and is thought to lift mood, with time or distance increased gradually.

depth.why: It builds a habit of regular runs that adds routine and a sense of progress.

perception.why: You keep a conversational pace by the talk test, running outdoors or on a treadmill.

guide.why: Beginners often start with walk-run intervals and build up over weeks, alone, with a friend, in a club or in group running therapy.

body.why: It means making your muscles work against a load, keeping good form through a full range of motion.

exertion.why: Each set should feel hard by the last few repetitions, and heavier loads tend to build the most strength, with a minute or two of rest between sets.

arousal.why: Heavy lifting briefly pushes blood pressure up, but the main aim is stronger muscles rather than keeping the heart rate up, with rests between sets.

social.why: It can be done in a gym or at home, alone, with a coach or in a class.

structure.why: Sessions are built from set exercises, sets of about 6 to 15 repetitions, planned rests and progressive overload.

stance.why: Progressive overload raises the load gradually as you get stronger, adding weight or repetitions as it gets easier.

depth.why: Its focus is getting measurably stronger week by week.

perception.why: You work against free weights, machines, bands or your own body weight, picking a weight that feels hard by the last few repetitions.

guide.why: It needs little space or equipment and can be done alone, though beginners benefit from instruction in technique.

body.why: You might sit with, stroke or play with a calm dog while talking through something hard, or take part in sessions with a horse.

exertion.why: Most programs use dogs, about 7 in 10, with activities such as sitting with, stroking or playing with them.

arousal.why: A calm, friendly animal is thought to ease stress and anxiety and make it easier to open up.

social.why: Sessions bring together a professional, often a handler and a trained animal whose companionship is thought to be an active ingredient, and horse-based work with veterans suggests bonding and peer support.

structure.why: It is planned, goal-directed treatment with goals set in advance and progress tracked as in any other therapy.

stance.why: It works toward goals set in advance, such as easing anxiety or building trust, with the animal's companionship as an active ingredient.

depth.why: It works toward goals such as easing anxiety, building trust or practicing social skills, and you may talk through something hard while stroking a dog.

perception.why: The work is done with a trained animal, most often a dog or a horse, by sitting with, stroking or playing with it or working alongside it.

guide.why: It is led by a health, education or human-service professional, and anyone who needs treatment should look for a licensed professional who offers it rather than a visiting program alone.

body.why: It works through posture, slow movement and breathing, with attention resting on the body.

exertion.why: It is gentle, low-impact exercise: slow forms such as Baduanjin, or still standing and seated postures.

arousal.why: Slow movement, slow breathing and meditative attention are thought to shift the nervous system toward rest, and some trials report lower heart rate and blood pressure.

social.why: It is usually learned in a group class and then practiced at home, alone or in a group.

structure.why: Most sessions follow a set sequence of simple, repeated movements, such as the eight movements of Baduanjin.

stance.why: It coordinates and regulates body, breath and mind, which traditional Chinese medicine explains as cultivating and balancing qi, through gentle exercise.

depth.why: It works with posture, movement, breath and a calm, focused mind.

perception.why: Attention rests on the body as you move in time with the breath, and static forms hold postures with breath awareness.

guide.why: It is usually learned from a trained instructor in a group class and then practiced at home.

body.why: It works through conversations, shared activities and regular contact with other people.

exertion.why: Typical contact means calls, meals, chats and groups such as a club, class, choir, team or volunteer shift.

arousal.why: It means regular contact and meeting new people, and nerves can get in the way, with intense fear or panic for some.

social.why: The practice is deliberately making regular time for other people.

structure.why: There is no agreed dose: you choose a few kinds of contact you can repeat, put them in your calendar and follow up with people.

stance.why: It is a deliberate change of habits: saying yes to invitations more often and comparing how each interaction went with what you expected.

depth.why: It is about making regular time for friends, family, neighbors and groups in everyday life.

perception.why: It is made of real contact, from a weekly call or meal to small daily exchanges with neighbors or shop staff.

guide.why: It is an everyday practice rather than a branded method, though in some countries health services can refer you to a social prescribing link worker.

body.why: It is walking in green or blue places, with attention drifting to sights, sounds and smells.

exertion.why: It pairs gentle to vigorous exercise, from a short park stroll to hours of steady effort on a long hike, and can feel like a break rather than a workout.

arousal.why: Natural settings are thought to calm body and mood and to hold attention gently, as stress reduction and attention restoration theories describe.

social.why: People walk alone, with friends or with a walking group, and walking with others adds social contact.

structure.why: You walk regularly in green or blue places, from a park loop near home to longer hikes that add route planning and navigation.

stance.why: Natural settings are thought to hold attention gently and give a sense of being away, so that tired attention can recover.

depth.why: It is time away from traffic, screens and daily demands, and nature walks may interrupt brooding.

perception.why: Attention drifts to what you see, hear and smell outdoors, and forest bathing uses each of the senses on purpose.

guide.why: You walk alone, with friends or with a walking group, and in the UK some health services refer people to nature-based group programs.

body.why: It gives full, open attention to raw sensory experience, including what you feel in the body, without getting lost in thoughts about it.

exertion.why: Exercises are done sitting or lying, as in the body scan, or while eating a raisin or listening to sounds.

arousal.why: It is used to settle and come back to the present, and attending to what you can sense now is thought to interrupt worry and rumination.

social.why: In MBSR the exercises are taught in weekly group classes, with about 45 minutes of daily home practice.

structure.why: It uses set exercises, such as the body scan, the raisin exercise and mindful listening, done with slow, curious attention.

stance.why: Attention is open and non-judging, and when the mind wanders into thought you notice this without judging it and return to your senses.

depth.why: It turns attention to what you can sense right now, and the aim is simple contact with the present.

perception.why: The senses themselves are the deliberate anchor: sight, sound, touch, taste, smell and body sensation.

guide.why: Single exercises can be practiced on your own at any time.

body.why: It works through sound, rhythm and movement as well as lyrics and talking about what came up.

exertion.why: Typical uses are listening, singing, playing simple instruments and moving to rhythm and music.

arousal.why: Music can shift mood and arousal, and music interventions lower both physical signs of stress, such as heart rate, and felt stress.

social.why: It ranges from listening alone to choirs, bands and group music therapy.

structure.why: A therapist sets goals and then uses varied music experiences, from improvising and songwriting to listening to chosen music.

stance.why: People listen on purpose to relax or ease anxiety, while active and receptive methods are used to express and explore feelings.

depth.why: It works with the feelings music stirs, and therapy uses it as a way to express and work through feelings.

perception.why: It centers on listening to and making real sound, and Guided Imagery and Music pairs listening with imagery.

guide.why: Clinical work calls for a credentialed music therapist, while self-directed use ranges from chosen listening to choir or band rehearsals.
